title: energy firms face ai enhanced cyber attacks connectivity push  reeii 2026 09 01
text:
September 1 - Energy companies are at risk from AI-aided cyber attacks, as vast networks of power generation, transmission and distribution have been digitalized and interconnected, effectively offering a large attack surface for hackers.
Ukraine’s energy infrastructure has been systematically targeted by Russian hackers since the start of the Russia-Ukraine war, and Poland has faced similar attacks, including one in December ​that aimed to disrupt the communication between renewable energy installations and power distribution operators.
Last month, U.S. officials warned unidentified hackers were trying to breach devices made by Siemens that are used across multiple critical infrastructure ‌sectors, including energy and manufacturing. Following media reports that Iran-linked hackers had shut down a small British energy facility, the UK in late August briefed energy company chiefs on steps to protect their assets, saying there was no threat to the wider electricity system.
Researchers at British cybersecurity company Bridewell said RomCom, a Russian-aligned hacking group, very likely used AI to generate social engineering content to target organizations in Critical National Infrastructure (CNI) sectors in the U.K. in 2025.
These attacks illustrate how hacking groups, many of which are affiliated with hostile governments such as Russia, Iran, and China, are increasingly targeting ​companies across critical infrastructure and many are relying on AI to increase the number and sophistication of their exploits, sources said.
CHART: Cyber attacks per week per energy organization
Some of these hackers are using ​AI to build scripts that attack operational technology assets, such as programmable logic controllers used across power generation facilities, as well as substations that control the flow of power.
“Those have been ⁠created by Iranian-aligned actors and are being used as part of that ever-increasing volume of attacks we're seeing,” Phil Tonkin, Field Chief Technology Officer at Dragos, a leading cybersecurity firm, told Reuters Events.
Large language models (LLMs) allow hackers without technical know-how to “automate a ​large percentage of a typical attack path,” hence “lowering the resources, time, and expertise” needed to carry out attacks, said Rob Denaburg, Senior Manager for Cybersecurity at the American Public Power Association, which represents 1,400 community-owned, not-for-profit public power utilities in the United States.
Operational ​technology assets use protocols to communicate. “AI is enabling people to design attacks that can speak the protocol language without having to take the time to become basically an engineer to learn how to do all that,” Denaburg said.

AI tools are also being used to identify vulnerabilities in energy systems, allowing adversaries to “increase the speed, the scale, and the efficiency of their attacks,” said Kieran Bhardwaj, Director of Technical Services at Bridewell.
Attackers rely on AI to sort through “large amounts of information of all the different potential targets they could take ​out there, and find out which ones are vulnerable in just the right ways at just the right times,” Bhardwaj said.
Cyber attackers can deploy AI tools to create a so-called “Cyber Kill Chain” to map the sequential vulnerabilities that can be targeted to ​carry out a successful exploit, Denaburg said.
Budget constraints, older assets
Large energy companies have bolstered their cybersecurity because they are increasingly aware of the dangers, but smaller utilities are “easy prey,” said Leo Simonovich, VP and Global Head, Industrial Cyber and Digital Security at Siemens Energy.
“If you look ‌at the United ⁠States, once you go outside the top 100, there are a bunch of small utilities that are facing the challenge, and those folks are what I would consider to be the weakest link,” Simonovich told Reuters Events.
Smaller U.S. utilities, especially those that operate in rural areas, lack the resources to rapidly scale their cyber defenses and even though they may hire the services of cybersecurity companies, they lack a dedicated workforce to implement safety measures around the clock, Denaburg said.

Older equipment that lacks programmable security features is more vulnerable to hacking.
“I don't think budget is necessarily the be-all and end-all of this challenge. I would actually say the amount of legacy equipment an organization has is a ​much more indicative stance to how hard their cyber security ​maturity journey is going to be,” Bhardwaj said.
And while large ⁠generation plants often feature “some very sophisticated” cybersecurity controls, renewable energy facilities that “typically just connect straight to the internet with one layer of control” are also vulnerable to attacks, Tonkin said.
For developers, “it's not easy to justify expenditure on sophisticated monitoring, or multiple firewalls” when they are building and operating a small solar farm, he said.
Security guidelines
To boost their defenses in the face of increasing cyberattacks, ​smaller utilities should perform an asset inventory to identify weaknesses, embed monitoring and detection, enable software updates and test patches, Simonovich said.
The energy industry could benefit from “blueprints” of standardized ​cybersecurity measures that all equipment manufacturers would ⁠have to follow, he added.
For example, Siemens is working with global risk management company DNV to produce cybersecurity standards for offshore wind turbines.

Tonkin said that although cybersecurity experts sometimes want to deploy “sophisticated standards with hundreds of controls,” the SANS Five Industrial Control Systems (ICS) Cybersecurity Critical Controls, are a reliable set of safeguards to secure critical infrastructure.
This framework created by the Sans Institute, a for-profit cybersecurity training company, focuses on dedicated incident response, defensible network architecture, continuous passive monitoring, secure remote access, and ⁠risk-based vulnerability mitigation.
Other public ​and private groups such as the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), the American Public Power Association, and OffSec, offer cybersecurity training courses and materials.
Energy companies ​could also deploy AI tools to identify and patch vulnerabilities, and to put up “strategic blockers” to neutralize “Cyber Kill Chains.”
“AI can be really good for helping prioritize where you might make limited investments,” Denaburg said.
But preventive work is time consuming and slow because companies often need to test patches to ensure that they ​won’t cause “any unpredictable or unexpected behavior in your system, which could end up disrupting power,” Denaburg noted.
“It's a bit of an uphill battle. Defenders have to be right 100 percent of the time, and attackers only have to be right once,” he said.
